name: Carl Friedrich Abel
description: Carl Friedrich Abel, a German viol player and composer, spent most of his career in London. There, together with Johann Christian Bach, he established a series of public concerts that helped shape the city's musical life. One of the last great virtuosos of the viola da gamba, he also wrote for keyboard, orchestra and chamber ensembles. His music reflects the transition from the Baroque idiom to the galant style.

name: John Adams
description: John Adams draws on the repetitive processes of minimalism while combining them with expansive orchestral writing and a dramatic sense of theatre inherited from opera. His works address American political history as well as intimate and mythological subjects. He has helped renew contemporary opera and American orchestral music.

name: Isaac Albéniz
description: The Catalan pianist and composer Isaac Albéniz helped renew Spanish music by bringing the rhythms, modes and colours of folk traditions into a pianistic language shaped by Liszt and French Romanticism. His best-known work, Iberia, turns the piano into an instrument of remarkable orchestral richness. He also wrote operas and numerous salon pieces, but his legacy rests above all on his mature works.

name: William Alwyn
description: British composer, flautist and teacher William Alwyn wrote symphonies, concertos, operas and film scores. His style evolved from neoclassicism towards a freer, more chromatic idiom, underpinned by formidable orchestral craftsmanship. He was one of the most prolific film composers in Britain.

name: Louis Andriessen
description: Louis Andriessen was a central figure in contemporary Dutch music. Breaking with Romantic and serial orchestral traditions, he forged an energetic, repetitive and politically engaged language shaped by jazz, Stravinsky and popular music. He often favoured unusual amplified ensembles, in which pulse and instrumental colour became structural forces. His influence on European new-music scenes was considerable.

name: Grażyna Bacewicz
description: Grażyna Bacewicz was a Polish composer and violinist whose work occupies a major place in 20th-century Central European music. Trained in Warsaw and Paris, she developed a language combining neoclassical clarity, rhythmic drive and increasingly adventurous harmonic exploration. Her dual career as performer and composer gave her instrumental writing an especially idiomatic character, notably in her concertos and chamber music.

name: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach
description: The second son of Johann Sebastian Bach, Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach studied with [[bach|his father Johann Sebastian Bach]] before pursuing a career that took him from Berlin, where he served Frederick the Great, to Hamburg, where he succeeded Telemann as director of music. He became a leading exponent of the empfindsamer Stil, or sensitive style, with its emotional contrasts, unpredictable turns and almost improvisatory eloquence. His keyboard writing profoundly reshaped the sonata and influenced Haydn, Mozart and later generations. A respected theorist, he published an essential treatise on the art of keyboard playing. His aesthetic stands at the crossroads of the late Baroque and emerging Classical style.

description: The youngest son of [[bach|Johann Sebastian Bach]] first received his musical training within the family before travelling to Italy to study vocal music and opera. After converting to Catholicism, he became organist at Milan Cathedral and established himself as an opera composer. From 1762 he was based in London, where he gained an international reputation. His elegant, melodic and balanced style helped spread the galant taste and the emerging Classical idiom. He met the young [[mozart|Mozart]] in London in 1764 and had a significant influence on him, especially in the keyboard concerto.

name: Johann Sebastian Bach
description: Born into a Thuringian family of musicians, Johann Sebastian Bach worked as an organist and court musician before becoming cantor of St Thomas's Church in Leipzig in 1723. His activity was closely tied to the institutions that employed him: he wrote cantatas, Passions and motets for the liturgical calendar, as well as instrumental and chamber works. He absorbed German, Italian and French traditions and transformed them through extraordinary contrapuntal density. Long known mainly to specialists after his death, his music was rediscovered in the 19th century, notably through Mendelssohn, and became a central reference point for Western musical thought.

description: British guitarist Derek Bailey was a founding figure of European free improvisation. Rejecting predetermined harmonic and rhythmic frameworks, he developed a practice grounded in the instant, attentive listening and the physical exploration of his instrument. As co-founder of the Incus label, he helped build an independent international scene.

name: Béla Bartók
description: Béla Bartók was a composer, pianist and ethnomusicologist. Together with Zoltán Kodály, he collected and studied the folk music of Central and Eastern Europe, transforming its rhythms, modes and structures into a deeply personal modern language. His music combines rhythmic energy, formal rigour, timbral exploration and expressive power. He is one of the major composers of the 20th century, both for his quartets and for his orchestral and piano works.

name: François Bayle
description: François Bayle is a major composer of acousmatic music and one of the leading theorists of spatial listening. Born in Madagascar, he joined Pierre Schaeffer's Groupe de recherches musicales and developed the concept of the acousmonium, an orchestra of loudspeakers designed to perform works on fixed media. His music explores sonic images, imaginary spaces and transformations of perception. He made a profound contribution to the aesthetic autonomy of electroacoustic music.

name: Ludwig van Beethoven
description: Educated in Bonn and later based in Vienna, Ludwig van Beethoven first made his name as a pianist and improviser before becoming one of the most influential composers of his age. His music moves beyond the Classical inheritance of [[haydn|Haydn]] and [[mozart|Mozart]] and opens new paths towards Romanticism. His progressive deafness, profound by the beginning of the 19th century, transformed his life without stopping his creative work. His late sonatas, quartets and Missa solemnis explore forms of striking originality. The Ninth Symphony, with its choral finale, expands the ambitions of the symphonic genre.

description: Dutch drummer and percussionist Han Bennink combines virtuosity, humour, physical energy and the subversion of everyday objects. A key figure in the European improvised-music scene, he collaborated with Misha Mengelberg, Brötzmann and Bailey. Furniture and found objects also become rhythmic and theatrical sound sources.

name: Alban Berg
description: Alban Berg brought together the Romantic inheritance and the radical language of atonality and later twelve-tone composition. A pupil of Schoenberg, he retained a lyrical and dramatic expressiveness that makes his music distinctive within the Second Viennese School. His two operas, Wozzeck and Lulu, are among the great works of 20th-century music theatre. His Violin Concerto, “To the Memory of an Angel”, has become one of the most frequently performed concertos of modernism.

description: Luciano Berio was one of the great innovators of post-war music. Co-founder of the Studio di Fonologia in Milan, he explored electronics, collage, quotation and the transformation of the voice. His Sequenze form a laboratory of virtuosity and instrumental invention, while Sinfonia examines musical memory and the coexistence of multiple languages.

description: Gilles de Bins, known as Binchois, was one of the leading figures of the Burgundian School. A singer and composer in the service of the Burgundian court, he developed a refined art of courtly song, marked by melodic clarity, elegant lines and restrained expressiveness. His sacred music also demonstrates the contrapuntal mastery of musicians of his time. Alongside Dufay, he helped shape the musical taste of 15th-century European courts.

name: Hildegard of Bingen
description: Hildegard of Bingen was an extraordinary figure of the 12th century: a Benedictine abbess, visionary author, theologian, naturalist and composer. Leading communities of women along the Rhine, she created a body of work in which poetry, symbolic thought and music form an indivisible whole. Her surviving musical corpus comprises around 77 liturgical chants, most with texts written by Hildegard herself, as well as the morality play Ordo Virtutum. Her melodies, often unusually wide-ranging and richly ornamented, extend beyond the customary contours of chant in her time. Their singularity also lies in the way the vocal line follows the imagery and movement of the text.

description: Born in Lucca into a family of musicians, Luigi Boccherini was a virtuoso cellist and composer. After periods in Vienna and Paris, he settled in Spain in the service of the Infante Don Luis, and later worked for several European patrons. He made a major contribution to the development of chamber music, especially the string quintet with two cellos, a formation whose possibilities he explored with great inventiveness. His instrumental writing is distinguished by elegant lines, rich dialogue between voices and an especially expressive role for the cello.

name: Anthony Braxton
description: Anthony Braxton is a saxophonist, improviser, educator and composer. Emerging from Chicago's experimental scene, he became involved with the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians (AACM), which championed aesthetic and institutional autonomy for African American musicians. His work reaches far beyond the categories of jazz: he has developed an immense system of compositions, graphic languages, diagrams and improvised structures. The Ghost Trance Music series, his orchestral compositions and his operatic cycles embody a mode of thought that is both systematic and open, closely interweaving improvisation, notation and collaboration.

name: William Byrd
description: William Byrd was one of the greatest English composers of the Renaissance. Despite the confessional tensions of Elizabethan England, he wrote for both Anglican institutions and clandestine Catholic communities. His output spans sacred and secular vocal music, keyboard works and consort music. He combined exceptional contrapuntal learning with an often sombre expressiveness, especially evident in his Latin motets and keyboard pieces.

name: Francesca Caccini
description: Francesca Caccini, known as la Cecchina, was a composer, singer and instrumentalist at the Medici court in Florence. The daughter of Giulio Caccini, she became one of the most remarkable musicians of her time and took an active part in the invention of Baroque music theatre. Her opera La liberazione di Ruggiero dall'isola d'Alcina, premiered in 1625, is the earliest known opera composed by a woman. Her career reveals the real, though often obscured, place of women in court musical institutions.

His collection Le nuove musiche set out a new approach to sung text, based on basso continuo, ornamentation and expressive declamation. name: John Cage
description: John Cage studied, among others, with [[schoenberg|Arnold Schoenberg]], but soon moved away from traditional ideas of composition. From the 1940s onwards, he explored percussion, prepared instruments, chance operations inspired by the I Ching and indeterminacy. His celebrated 4′33″ shifts attention away from the musical object towards listening to the sounds present in a given situation. Close to New York's avant-garde artists, he collaborated with choreographers such as Merce Cunningham and profoundly influenced visual art, performance and experimental practice. Rather than defining what music is, his work questions the very conditions of listening.

description: Born in Florence, Luigi Cherubini studied in Italy before settling in Paris in 1788. He became a central figure in the city's musical life, lived through the Revolution and the Empire, and directed the Paris Conservatoire from 1822 to 1842. His style combines the Italian contrapuntal tradition with a dramatic approach shaped by [[gluck|Gluck]] and French opera. His operas, especially Médée, are admired for their tension and demanding vocal writing. He also composed a substantial body of sacred music, including masses and requiems that were long held in the highest esteem.

description: Born in Żelazowa Wola near Warsaw, Frédéric Chopin left Poland in 1830 and settled in Paris, where he became a central figure in musical life and the salons. He composed almost exclusively for the piano, yet profoundly renewed its language: virtuosity became expression, dance forms turned into poetic structures, and harmony ventured into new colours. His mazurkas and polonaises maintain a complex relationship with the rhythms and memories of his homeland. His relationship with George Sand marked a long period of creativity, especially at Nohant. His music permanently reshaped the technique and poetry of piano writing.

His fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets form an immense musical diary of the century, while his operas and concertos reveal exceptional orchestral and instrumental imagination.

Trained at the Conservatorio di Santa Maria di Loreto, he quickly found success in Naples before working in several European cities, notably St Petersburg and Vienna. His music theatre is distinguished by lively ensembles, comic energy and subtle characterisation. He also wrote serious operas and instrumental music. His virtuosity helped establish the piano as a central instrument of modern musical life. His sonatas explore the range, power and technical possibilities of the new instrument, and their inventiveness was admired by [[beethoven|Beethoven]]. His work as a publisher and piano maker contributed to the development of instrument building and the music market. Gradus ad Parnassum became a cornerstone of piano pedagogy.

His language transformed harmony, form and orchestration through modes, non-functional chords, timbre and resonance. Though often associated with Impressionism, he rejected the label. Against conventions that prized vocal virtuosity for its own sake, he advocated a more continuous dramaturgy in which overture, chorus, dance and recitative contributed to the unity of the drama. description: Japanese trumpeter Toshinori Kondo developed a practice at the intersection of free jazz, improvisation and electronics. Live processing transforms the trumpet's timbre into textures approaching synthesis. His collaborations with Brötzmann, Bill Laswell and other musicians connect experimental scenes in Japan, Europe and the United States.

name: Helmut Lachenmann
description: Helmut Lachenmann studied in Stuttgart and later with Luigi Nono in Venice. He developed what he called instrumental concrete music: rather than treating instruments simply as producers of notes, he explores the gestures, friction, breath, resistance and noise through which sound becomes possible. This approach transforms listening and reveals the physical and social conditions of musical practice. Demanding of performers and audiences alike, his work does not seek novelty for its own sake; it questions perceptual habits and conventions inherited from the concert tradition.

description: Florentine composer, organist and poet Francesco Landini was the most celebrated figure of the Italian Trecento. His two- and three-part ballate combine melodic suppleness, contrapuntal refinement and courtly poetry. His music is essential to understanding the flowering of Italian secular music before the Renaissance.

description: György Ligeti lived through several of the major transformations in music during the second half of the 20th century. After fleeing Hungary in 1956, he joined the electronic music studios in Cologne, then developed an instrumental language based on sound masses, micropolyphony and transformations of texture. His music eludes schools and serial orthodoxies. He also explored polyrhythms, absurd mechanisms and perceptual illusions.

description: American composer Alvin Lucier explored acoustic phenomena, resonance, brain waves and the physical properties of spaces. His work lies at the intersection of experimental music, installation and sound art. Rather than composing traditional musical objects, he created situations in which sound reveals phenomena that normally remain imperceptible. description: Witold Lutosławski was one of the major Polish composers of the 20th century. His style evolved from neoclassicism towards a personal language based on controlled aleatory, mobile textures and exceptional orchestral command. He devised systems in which performers enjoy rhythmic freedom within a carefully structured framework. His orchestral and concertante works rank among the great achievements of post-war contemporary music.

name: Guillaume de Machaut
description: As much a poet as a musician, Guillaume de Machaut served as secretary and cleric to powerful lords, notably John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia, and later the court of Navarre. His work, carefully transmitted in often richly illuminated manuscripts, offers one of the earliest authorial bodies of music in Europe. He wrote in the fixed forms — ballade, rondeau and virelai — as well as the motet and liturgical music. His Messe de Nostre Dame is one of the earliest complete polyphonic mass cycles attributed to a single composer. His art combines contrapuntal architecture, formal virtuosity and an intense relationship between poetry and music.

His five books of viol pieces form a vast repertoire documenting the evolution of French chamber music under Louis XIV and the Regency.

His extensive catalogue spans symphonies, operas, concertos and chamber music, in a modern style that is mobile and luminous.

He wrote madrigals, operas, sacred music and ballets. L'Orfeo (1607) is among the earliest great surviving operas. In his later books of madrigals, voice, instrument and basso continuo become the actors in miniature dramas of unprecedented intensity.

After years in the service of the Archbishop of Salzburg, he settled in Vienna as an independent musician, an audacious and precarious position. He composed in almost every genre of his time: opera, symphony, concerto, chamber music, serenade and sacred music. His music theatre observes social and psychological relationships with exceptional subtlety, while his instrumental music combines formal balance and intensity. His final opera, The Magic Flute, and the unfinished Requiem belong to the last months of his life.

His reputation was immense: music printing helped spread his masses, motets and chansons throughout Europe. His teaching brought him into contact with several generations of musicians, including [[beethoven|Beethoven]], [[schubert|Schubert]] and Liszt.
